faq.q: Why does a petechial rash appear in fat embolism?

faq.a: Yes, severe pancreatitis, burns, or sickle‑cell bone infarction can release fat into circulation.
faq.q: Can fat embolism occur without a fracture?

faq.a: Evidence is mixed; steroids may reduce incidence in high‑risk orthopaedic patients but increase infection risk, so use selectively.

exam: A 25‑year‑old male with a femur fracture develops tachypnoea and confusion 24 h later – what is the most likely diagnosis and which clinical criteria confirm it? — Fat embolism syndrome; Gurd’s criteria (≥2 major or 1 major + ≥2 minor).
What bedside investigations would you perform if a CT scanner is unavailable? — ABG for hypoxia, chest auscultation, CBC for thrombocytopenia, and bedside ultrasound for pleural effusion.
How does the management of FES differ from that of a pulmonary embolism? — FES focuses on supportive O₂, fracture stabilisation, and avoiding anticoagulation; PE requires anticoagulation.
Which finding helps distinguish FES from sepsis‑related ARDS? — Presence of petechial rash and falling platelet count in FES; sepsis usually has fever and positive cultures.
Why is early external fixation of long‑bone fractures important in preventing FES? — It reduces intramedullary pressure and limits fat entry into circulation.
A patient with sickle‑cell disease presents with bone pain and sudden hypoxia – what additional cause should you consider? — Fat embolism from bone infarction.
What red‑flag sign would prompt immediate intubation in a patient with suspected FES? — PaO₂ < 50 mmHg despite high‑flow O₂ or signs of respiratory fatigue.
When would corticosteroids be justified in FES, and what is a major contraindication? — Consider in high‑risk orthopaedic trauma where infection risk is low; contraindicated in active sepsis.
ai.title: Fat Embolism Syndrome
ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: Fat embolism syndrome (FES) is a rapid, potentially fatal complication of long‑bone fracture or other fat‑rich tissue injury, causing respiratory distress, neurological change and petechial rash. Diagnosis relies on clinical criteria; early supportive care and prevention are key.

b: Gurd’s criteria (≥2 major or 1 major + ≥2 minor) are widely used.
Major: respiratory distress, cerebral signs, petechial rash.
Minor: tachycardia, fever, retinal fat emboli, thrombocytopenia, anemia, elevated ESR.
sections.p: FES is a clinical syndrome caused by fat globules entering the bloodstream, most often after fractures of the femur or pelvis, leading to pulmonary, neurologic and dermatologic manifestations.

b: Mild: oxygen saturation > 90 % on room air.
Moderate: PaO₂ < 60 mmHg or SpO₂ < 90 % requiring supplemental O₂.
Severe: PaO₂ < 50 mmHg, need for mechanical ventilation, or hemodynamic instability.
sections.p: Severity is staged by clinical progression: early (within 12‑24 h, mild hypoxia), intermediate (24‑72 h, worsening hypoxia, confusion), late (≥72 h, multiorgan failure).

b: Long‑bone or pelvic fracture (most common).
Severe burns or crush injuries.
Orthopaedic surgery (intramedullary nailing).
Pancreatitis (systemic inflammation).
Sepsis (especially Gram‑negative).
Sickle‑cell vaso‑occlusive crisis with bone infarction.
sections.p: Fat emboli arise from disruption of marrow fat, but several conditions common in low‑resource settings increase risk.

b: Dyspnoea, tachypnoea, diffuse crackles.
Confusion, agitation, seizures, or coma.
Petechiae on conjunctiva, oral mucosa, chest or upper limbs.
Fever, tachycardia, anemia, thrombocytopenia.
sections.p: The classic triad appears 12‑72 h after injury: respiratory distress, neurological alteration, and a petechial rash, but any component may dominate.

t.b: Is there hypoxemia? – PaO₂ < 60 mmHg confirms respiratory compromise.
Shows diffuse bilateral infiltrates; if unavailable, rely on clinical hypoxia and auscultation.
Excludes pulmonary embolism; may show ground‑glass opacities typical of FES.
Detects anemia and thrombocytopenia; falling platelets support diagnosis.
Elevated levels suggest fat overload but are not diagnostic.

b: PaO₂ < 50 mmHg despite O₂ therapy.
Unexplained seizures or coma.
Persistent hypotension requiring vasopressors.
Multiorgan failure (renal, hepatic).
sections.p: Rapid progression to severe hypoxia, refractory shock, or cerebral edema signals imminent death.

b: Stabilise fractures early; use external fixation when possible.
Supplemental O₂; intubate if PaO₂ < 50 mmHg or respiratory fatigue.
Fluid optimisation – avoid overload; use crystalloids.
Consider corticosteroids (e.g., methylprednisolone) only in centres where benefit outweighs infection risk.
Analgesia with non‑opioid agents; avoid high‑dose NSAIDs if renal impairment.
sections.p: Treat the source, provide supportive care, and monitor for deterioration.

b: Repeat chest imaging before discharge.
Neuro‑assessment at 2‑week and 6‑week visits.
Physiotherapy to improve lung volumes.
Educate patients on early reporting of dyspnoea or confusion.
sections.p: After acute phase, monitor pulmonary function and neurocognitive recovery; early mobilisation reduces later embolic risk.

b: Pulmonary embolism – usually sudden onset, no rash, normal platelets.
Acute respiratory distress syndrome from sepsis – lacks petechiae, often associated with infection source.
Meningococcemia – prominent purpuric rash, positive blood cultures.
sections.p: Conditions sharing respiratory or neurologic signs can mimic FES.

b: Chest X‑ray can be normal in first 12 h; rely on clinical picture.
Platelet count may stay normal until 48 h; watch trend.
ABG may show only mild hypoxia early; repeat if symptoms worsen.
sections.p: Certain investigations may be normal early, giving false reassurance.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden drop in oxygen saturation below 90 % despite O₂.
